Set telemetry budgets and review log ingestion, retention, Prometheus cardinality, scrape frequency, and duplicate collection. Use data collection rules, ConfigMap filters, and supported metric profiles to retain the signals needed for security, SLOs, and investigations.

Choose log table plans and retention based on query, alerting, export, and compliance needs, not ingestion price alone. Validate dashboards and alerts after every collection change. Dropping audit records or verbose application logs can reduce cost but also remove evidence that can't be recreated later.

items.text: Keep admission webhooks available and rehearse safe recovery
items.description:
Applicability: Applies when mutating or validating admission webhooks are installed, including policy, service mesh and extension webhooks.

Inventory admission webhook dependencies and operate highly available backends with tested API-server reachability, healthy endpoints and valid serving certificates/CA trust. Monitor admission latency and errors and verify that backend loss cannot unexpectedly block cluster recovery or silently bypass required policy.

Review timeoutSeconds and failurePolicy for each webhook: Fail protects enforcement but can block writes during an outage, while Ignore preserves availability at the cost of bypass risk. Scope namespace/object selectors and resource rules narrowly, especially for system components and the webhook's own recovery dependencies; document reviewed exclusions rather than broadly disabling controls. Test node drains, certificate rotation, network restrictions and Kubernetes upgrades, and rehearse a tightly authorized, audited emergency recovery procedure with restoration of enforcement.

items.text: Validate resilience with controlled fault injection under load
items.description:
Applicability: Applies to workloads with availability or recovery targets that require evidence of behavior during component and dependency failures.

Run hypothesis-driven resilience tests under representative load, beginning in an isolated nonproduction environment. Measure availability, latency, recovery time and data integrity against workload SLOs while injecting bounded pod, node, network and dependency faults. Record failures and verify remediation.

Define an approved blast radius, steady-state metrics, abort thresholds, rollback/recovery steps, owners and observation coverage before each experiment. Include saturation, timeouts, retry amplification, scaling and dependency throttling where relevant. Production fault injection is optional and requires separate risk approval and proven safety controls; never require destructive production chaos or delete production to satisfy this check. Operational fault testing complements disaster-recovery rebuild and restore drills.

items.text: Define non-functional requirements such as SLAs, RTO (Recovery Time Objective) and RPO (Recovery Point Objective)
items.description: Define workload availability SLOs, maximum tolerable data loss (RPO), and recovery time (RTO) before production. Cover pod, node, zone, regional, deletion, and corruption scenarios along with external dependencies. Choose architecture, replication, backup frequency, retention, and recovery capacity from these targets and validate them with measured drills rather than service SLA percentages alone.

items.text: Rehearse disaster recovery and clean-environment rebuilds regularly
items.description:
Rebuild into an isolated recovery environment from infrastructure as code, restore representative backups, and validate application and data integrity. Do not delete production to test recovery. Rehearse node, zone, and regional failures appropriate to the workload, and measure achieved RPO and RTO.

Keep versioned runbooks with recovery order, owners, credentials and break-glass access, DNS and traffic changes, validation gates, rollback, and failback. Test without relying on the failed region's pipelines, registry endpoints, secrets, or monitoring, and record remediation actions after drills.

items.text: Use Availability Zones if supported in your Azure region
items.description:
Applicability: Availability-sensitive workloads requiring resilience to an intra-region zone failure where the Azure region, node VM sizes, and dependencies support availability zones.

Where supported by region and VM SKU, distribute application node pools across availability zones and spread replicas across nodes and zones. Zones are separate datacenter failure domains within a region, not update domains in one datacenter. Align storage redundancy, load balancing, and recovery capacity; a zone-enabled cluster does not automatically make every workload or dependency zone-resilient.

items.text: Plan for multiregion deployment
items.description:
Applicability: Only workloads whose availability, RPO, RTO, or regulatory requirements require recovery in another region; multiple live regions are not required for every workload.

Select active-active, warm standby, or cold recovery from workload RPO/RTO, consistency, cost, and data residency requirements. Validate AKS, VM, storage, network, and quota availability in each target region and provision failover capacity. Region pairing is not mandatory for all architectures, but specific replication and Azure Backup Cross Region Restore capabilities depend on supported paired regions.

items.text: Create a data replication, recovery, and failback plan
items.description:
Applicability: Stateful workloads and external data dependencies whose RPO and RTO require data recovery or failover across failure domains; regional replication is needed only when regional recovery targets justify it.

Inventory persistent volumes and external data services and define supported replication or backup/restore for each according to RPO and RTO. Validate consistency and replication lag against RPO, including write fencing to avoid split-brain during failover. Measure recovery and failback time in drills, including data reconciliation and application restart order. Replication can propagate deletion and corruption and is not a substitute for independently retained backups.

items.text: Use Standard or Premium tier for production control-plane uptime SLA
items.description:
Use Standard tier for production cluster management, or Premium when long-term Kubernetes support is required. Standard and Premium include a Kubernetes API server uptime SLA of 99.95% with availability zones or 99.9% without, subject to current service terms. Free tier has no financially backed uptime SLA.

The control-plane SLA is not an end-to-end application availability guarantee. AKS Automatic is preconfigured with Standard tier and also has qualifying pod readiness SLA coverage under separate conditions; workload replicas, topology, storage, networking, and recovery still require design and testing.

items.text: Spread workload replicas across nodes and zones
items.description:
Applicability: Availability-sensitive workloads that need replicated serving capacity during node or zone failure; apply zone spreading where supported and required by the workload availability target.

Use topology spread constraints for kubernetes.io/hostname and topology.kubernetes.io/zone, or justified anti-affinity, to distribute replicas across failure domains. Match label selectors to the intended workload and ensure enough replicas and capacity remain after a domain failure.

Choose maxSkew and DoNotSchedule versus ScheduleAnyway deliberately. Strict rules can leave replacement pods pending when a zone or capacity is unavailable; test their interaction with volume topology, taints, autoscaling, and upgrades. Scheduling constraints do not automatically rebalance every already-running pod.

items.text: If using a private registry (ACR), configure region replication to store images in multiple regions
items.description:
Applicability: Multi-region recovery scenarios where AKS depends on a private registry and required container images must remain accessible during a regional outage.

For multi-region AKS deployments, evaluate ACR Premium geo-replication or another tested image-distribution strategy so recovery nodes can pull required digests during a regional outage.

ACR geo-replication is asynchronous and is not an independent backup against deletion or compromise. Confirm required images and OCI artifacts are available before regional rollout, configure private endpoints and DNS for replicas where needed, and test cold-node pulls during failover.

items.text: Verify registry regional zone support and data-plane resilience
items.description:
Applicability: Deployments using Azure Container Registry where registry availability is part of the workload's zone-resilience requirements.

ACR data-plane zone redundancy is enabled by default for all tiers in regions supporting availability zones, including existing registries and supported geo-replicas. Verify region support rather than requiring the legacy zoneRedundancy property to be Enabled; that property no longer controls behavior. ACR Tasks do not currently support availability zones, and zone redundancy does not protect against a region-wide outage.

items.text: Separate the registry lifecycle from disposable compute resources
items.description:
Applicability: Shared or recovery-critical registries whose artifacts must outlive disposable AKS environments.

Place shared registries in a resource group whose lifecycle is independent of disposable AKS environments. Apply least-privilege management access and appropriate resource locks to reduce accidental registry deletion.

Resource groups are lifecycle and management scopes, not backup boundaries. Registry resource locks do not prevent all data-plane artifact deletion; protect repository permissions and retain recoverable copies of critical release artifacts.

items.text: Evaluate ACR soft delete preview and compatible artifact recovery controls
items.description:
Applicability: Azure Container Registry deployments evaluating artifact deletion recovery where preview support terms and soft-delete compatibility limitations are acceptable.

Where preview use is acceptable, evaluate ACR soft delete with a tested 1-90 day retention and restore process. It currently does not support geo-replicated registries or artifact cache and cannot coexist with the retention policy. Retained artifacts incur storage charges. Use another compatible recovery strategy when these limitations conflict with regional resilience requirements.

Restore tests must include multi-architecture manifests and OCI referrers: restoring a manifest list or subject does not recursively restore child manifests or signatures. Soft delete is not an independent backup against registry deletion or compromise.

items.text: Select and test a supported recovery solution for cluster resources and data
items.description:
Applicability: Workloads with Kubernetes resources or durable data that must be recovered after loss, deletion, or corruption. Select coverage per volume type and external data service; Azure Backup-specific requirements apply only when that implementation is selected.

Select Azure Backup for AKS or another supported recovery solution that meets measured RPO, RTO, retention, and consistency requirements. Inventory Kubernetes resources, PV types, excluded data, and managed external data services; configure supported protection for each and test restores for data integrity and application readiness. Protect backup resources with a lifecycle independent of disposable clusters and source data. Document dependencies on snapshots, metadata, source accounts, and regions rather than treating replication or successful backup jobs as proof of recoverability.

When using Azure Backup, Operational backups use snapshots and extension metadata storage in your subscription; eligible Azure Disk backups can also transfer to the Vault tier, but a Backup vault does not mean all backup data is vaulted. Check the live support matrix: Azure Files SMB requires CSI driver 1.32+, is Operational-tier only with at most 30-day retention, and has network, file-count, and restore-location restrictions. NFS Files, Blob CSI, Azure Container Storage, and in-tree PVs are not covered. Enable CSI snapshots, supported managed identities, a healthy Linux backup extension, Trusted Access, and required networking/RBAC; don't co-install Velero with that extension. Snapshot backups are crash-consistent, not automatically application-consistent or atomic across volumes; use supported application hooks or database-native protection when needed. Protect excluded resources and external services separately and validate that source deletion cannot remove the only recovery copy.

items.text: Match backup tiers and cross-region restore to measured RPO and RTO
items.description:
Applicability: Only deployments selecting Azure Backup for AKS; assess Vault tier and Cross Region Restore only when their supported scenarios are needed to meet recovery requirements.

Validate backup cadence, completion, tiering, replication lag, and restore duration against recovery targets. Operational AKS backups have a minimum scheduled interval of four hours and restore within the source region. Vault-tier recovery points are daily for eligible Azure Disks; Cross Region Restore requires supported paired regions, a geo-redundant Backup vault, and Cross Region Restore enabled.

The current matrix describes up to 24-hour primary-region and up to 36-hour secondary-region vaulted RPO, not continuous point-in-time recovery. Vaulting is region-limited and currently supports at most 100 Azure Disk PVs per backup instance with disks no larger than 1 TB, public disk network access enabled, and no Disk Encryption Set or Microsoft Entra data-access authentication. Azure Files is not eligible. Do not weaken required security controls simply to enable vaulting; choose another supported recovery strategy when necessary. Test target-cluster capacity, compatible APIs, identities, networking, recovery order, and cleanup of staged restore resources.

items.text: Protect recovery points from deletion and monitor restore readiness
items.description:
Applicability: Only deployments using Azure Backup for AKS. For other recovery implementations, assess equivalent deletion protection, monitoring, and restore readiness under the recovery-solution control.

Separate backup administration from workload administration and evaluate supported vault immutability, enhanced soft delete, and multi-user authorization. Alert on backup failures, skipped volumes, stale recovery points, and vault-tier transfer failures. Validate restore permissions and recovery-point usability through drills.

Vault protections do not automatically protect Operational-tier snapshots or extension metadata in your subscription. Azure Files snapshots depend on the source share and account lifecycle. Confirm supported resource-lock behavior, deletion permissions, and retention for each storage type rather than treating successful configuration as ransomware protection.

items.text: Configure disruption budgets and test maintenance capacity
items.description:
Applicability: Replicated availability-sensitive workloads managed through the Eviction API during drains, upgrades, or consolidation; not a blanket requirement for restartable batch jobs or workloads that deliberately accept interruption.

Create separate policy/v1 PodDisruptionBudget objects with selectors matching replicated services and tested minAvailable or maxUnavailable values. Verify healthy replicas, allowed disruptions, and spare scheduling capacity so drains and upgrades can progress within the workload availability target. Test eviction behavior with unhealthy pods and measure drain completion time; configure readiness, rollout strategy, replicas, and topology separately.

PDBs constrain voluntary Eviction API operations such as normal node drains, not hardware or zone failures, direct pod deletion, or Deployment and StatefulSet rolling updates. Involuntary disruptions can reduce the remaining disruption allowance but aren't prevented by the budget. A zero-disruption budget can block maintenance; permit at least one eviction where the workload allows it and document coordination when it doesn't. Consider unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow when an unhealthy pod would otherwise block draining, and test that policy against application recovery behavior. A PDB isn't an uptime guarantee.

Related controls: Implement a proper Readiness probe (de1b6b38-4fa9-4f6e-ab92-d824346dd20c); Implement graceful termination and use preStop hooks when needed (dc4828a3-fc4f-4ac5-8844-122b8482dbb1); Spread workload replicas across nodes and zones (1eea4888-8c2a-40b2-a40b-cacdc5f55497)

items.text: Map the base image to node OS
items.description:
Applicability: Only deployments running or planning Windows container workloads on Windows node pools.

Use supported Windows Server 2022 or 2025 node images and validate the official host/container compatibility matrix. AKS supports process isolation, not Hyper-V isolation; don't assume all container image versions can run on every Windows host.

Windows Server 2019 support ended March 1, 2026 and it isn't supported on Kubernetes 1.33 or later. Select compatible node OS, Kubernetes, and container base image versions together, and use OS/build-aware scheduling when multiple Windows versions coexist.

items.text: Test Windows application shutdown and interrupted-work recovery
items.description:
Applicability: Only Windows container workloads whose shutdown and interrupted-work recovery must be validated during drains or termination.

Don't assume Linux signal-handling behavior applies to Windows. Test how the Windows runtime and application respond to termination, lifecycle hooks, and terminationGracePeriodSeconds during a real node drain. Choose sufficient shutdown time, stop accepting new requests, and make interrupted work recoverable.

items.text: Don't use privileged containers
items.description:
Applicability: Only deployments running ordinary Windows application containers; assess trusted host-level administration separately under the HostProcess control.

Ordinary Windows containers don't support Linux privileged-container mode. Use ContainerUser where the application permits and restrict host access. Windows HostProcess containers are a separate, highly privileged mechanism for trusted node administration, not a way to run ordinary application workloads.

items.text: Watch for memory usage
items.description:
Applicability: Only deployments running Windows nodes and container workloads.

Windows memory accounting, paging, and node-pressure behavior differ from Linux; don't rely on Linux OOM and eviction assumptions. Set measured memory requests and limits, monitor committed memory and paging as well as working set, and retain headroom for the OS and system services.

items.text: Choose a Windows-compatible Azure CNI network model
items.description:
Applicability: Only clusters with Windows node pools or a planned migration to Windows workloads.

Windows node pools require Azure CNI; kubenet and bring-your-own CNI aren't supported. Evaluate Azure CNI Overlay for address-space efficiency or a supported VNet-routable mode when direct pod addressing is required.

Check the Windows OS, Kubernetes version, and network policy engine compatibility together. Azure CNI powered by Cilium doesn't support Windows; a Linux-only networking recommendation must not be applied blindly to mixed-OS clusters.

items.text: Patch Windows hosts and rebuild container base images independently
items.description:
Applicability: Only deployments maintaining Windows node images or Windows container base images.

AKS publishes Windows node images monthly; Windows Update doesn't automatically patch these hosts. Apply node image upgrades through NodeImage automation or a monitored manual process, and separately rebuild and redeploy application images from patched Windows base images.

Node image upgrades don't update your application images. Test host/base-image compatibility and rolling drains before production, and don't assume matching monthly revision numbers are universally required across supported Windows versions. SecurityPatch isn't supported for Windows; Unmanaged behaves like None.

items.text: Secure the traffic of your containers
items.description:
Applicability: Only deployments running Windows workloads that require pod network isolation; affected Windows Network Policy Manager deployments must migrate to a supported implementation.

Apply least-privilege pod network policies with an engine supported for the exact Windows OS and network model, and verify enforcement with connectivity tests. Use application authentication and TLS as additional controls, not substitutes for network isolation.

Azure Network Policy Manager on Windows became unsupported on September 30, 2026. Cilium isn't supported on Windows; use the current AKS policy support matrix to evaluate Calico and validate any OS-version gaps before migration.

items.text: Use gMSA when Windows workloads require Active Directory authentication
items.description:
Applicability: Only Windows workloads requiring Active Directory domain authentication through a supported gMSA integration; workloads without this dependency do not need gMSA.

Use group Managed Service Accounts for applications that require Active Directory domain authentication. Configure the supported AKS integration, credential specifications, Key Vault access, and domain-controller connectivity with least privilege; don't enable gMSA for workloads that don't need it.

items.text: If required for AKS Windows workloads, HostProcess containers can be used
items.description:
Applicability: Only Windows deployments with a justified host-level administration or node-agent requirement that needs HostProcess access; not ordinary application containers.

Use Windows HostProcess containers only for trusted host-level administration such as node agents. They run in the host context with access beyond ordinary container isolation; constrain who can deploy them, use approved images, and audit their permissions and activity.

items.text: Taint Windows nodes
items.description:
Applicability: Only clusters containing Windows pools, including mixed-OS deployments where workloads must be scheduled onto compatible hosts.

Set kubernetes.io/os: windows selectors for Windows workloads and Linux selectors for Linux workloads; use Windows build labels or RuntimeClasses when container compatibility requires a specific host build. Taint Windows pools and grant tolerations only to intended workloads; a toleration alone doesn't select a Windows node.

items.text: Validate Calico policy support before migrating Windows network enforcement
items.description:
Applicability: Only Windows deployments using or evaluating AKS-managed Calico, including migrations from retired Windows Network Policy Manager; not a requirement to adopt Calico on other clusters.

AKS-managed Calico supports Kubernetes networking.k8s.io policies on documented Windows configurations. Validate the current OS/network compatibility matrix and test ingress, egress, DNS, and service traffic before replacing an existing policy engine.

The current network policy matrix lists Windows Server 2019 and 2022 for Calico; that doesn't restore support for retired Windows Server 2019 or establish support for Windows Server 2025. Verify the latter before migrating. AKS-managed Calico doesn't support projectcalico.org policies or running alongside Calico Cloud or Enterprise.

items.text: Verify Accelerated Networking on supported Windows VM sizes
items.description:
Applicability: Only Windows node pools using VM sizes, images, and drivers that support Accelerated Networking.

AKS enables Accelerated Networking on supported VM sizes. Verify VM, image, and driver support and benchmark network throughput and latency; don't modify AKS-managed NICs directly to force enablement on unsupported configurations.

items.text: Migrate retired Windows OS channels and plan supported LTSC upgrades
items.description:
Applicability: Only Windows deployments using retired OS channels or planning an LTSC migration before the documented support and image-removal deadlines.

Migrate Windows Server 2019, unsupported since March 1, 2026, before image removal on April 1, 2027. Windows Annual Channel preview support ended May 15, 2026, with image removal on May 15, 2027. Retired images eventually prevent scaling and remediation, not just security updates.

Evaluate Windows Server 2025 LTSC on Kubernetes 1.32 or later and test host/container compatibility, agents, gMSA, storage, and network policy first. Windows Server 2025 pools require FIPS-enabled images. Windows Server 2022 support ends June 30, 2028 and isn't available for Kubernetes 1.37 or later; images are removed June 30, 2029. A new-pool migration permits staged validation. The in-place 2022-to-2025 migration uses aks-preview and requires Kubernetes 1.32 to 1.36; assess its preview support terms before use.

items.text: Include Windows-specific capacity and observability in the operating model
items.description:
Applicability: Only clusters operating Windows user pools and their supporting Linux system pool, capacity, and monitoring integrations.

Maintain a Linux system pool alongside Windows user pools and include Windows startup, image-pull, patching, and drain times in capacity and maintenance tests. Windows pools aren't supported by NAP or AKS Automatic, so select a supported AKS Standard configuration.

For managed Prometheus, enable Windows recording rules and confirm Windows exporter metrics and Windows dashboards are populated. Monitor memory commitment, paging, storage, network errors, and application availability rather than relying only on Linux dashboards.

items.text: Implement a proper Liveness probe
items.description: Use a liveness probe when restarting the container can recover an unhealthy application. Check local process health rather than shared downstream dependencies to avoid restart storms during an outage. Tune timeouts and failure thresholds under realistic load; failed liveness probes restart the container according to its restart policy, not the entire pod.

items.text: Implement a proper Startup probe
items.description: Protect slow-starting containers with a startup probe. Liveness and readiness probes do not run until it succeeds. Set failureThreshold and periodSeconds to cover measured worst-case startup time, and test cold starts; exhausting the startup failure threshold triggers container restart according to its restart policy.

items.text: Implement a proper Readiness probe
items.description:
Applicability: Applies to availability-sensitive services receiving traffic through Kubernetes Services or other readiness-aware routing.

Use readiness probes to indicate whether the application can serve traffic. A failed readiness probe normally removes the pod from ready Service endpoints without restarting its containers. Test dependency failures and recovery without making every replica unready for an optional dependency; account for endpoint propagation, existing connections, and Services that publish not-ready addresses.

items.text: Implement graceful termination and use preStop hooks when needed
items.description:
Applicability: Applies to availability-sensitive services or workers that must drain requests or checkpoint work during planned termination.

Handle termination signals, stop accepting new work, and drain in-flight requests or checkpoint work within terminationGracePeriodSeconds. Add a preStop hook only when needed and include its execution time in the grace period. Hooks and graceful shutdown are not guaranteed during node loss, force deletion, or abrupt process failure; test rolling updates and node drains.

items.text: Run more than one replica for your Deployment
items.description:
Applicability: Applies to availability-sensitive services whose design permits concurrent replicas; singleton workloads require a separately tested recovery design.

Run multiple ready replicas for services that require availability during pod failure or maintenance. Size the replica count and autoscaler minimum for the availability target and remaining capacity after a failure. Spread replicas across nodes and, where available, zones; extra replicas on one node are not sufficient.

items.text: Apply consistent Kubernetes labels and Azure resource tags
items.description:
Apply recommended Kubernetes application labels and ownership/environment metadata for selectors, policy, operations, and cost allocation. Azure resource tags and Kubernetes labels are separate mechanisms and are not automatically synchronized. Keep secrets and personal data out of both.

Define technical, business and security metadata, including owner, environment, cost center and lifecycle. Apply Azure tags through supported AKS cluster and node pool APIs and review propagation and replacement behavior before updates; do not directly retag AKS-managed infrastructure to bypass those APIs. Define deliberate mappings to Kubernetes labels and validate selectors before changing labels used by controllers or policies.

items.text: Implement autoscaling of your applications (Horizontal pod autoscaler, KEDA)
items.description: Use HPA for resource, custom, or external metrics, or the managed KEDA add-on for event-driven scaling. Configure resource requests for utilization-based targets, minimum/maximum replicas, stabilization, and metric failure behavior. Load-test startup latency and downstream capacity; coordinate pod scaling with node capacity and quotas. Do not configure independent HPA and KEDA controllers for the same workload.

items.text: Use namespaces with explicit access and isolation controls
items.description:
Use dedicated namespaces rather than the default namespace for managed workloads. Apply scoped RBAC, network policies, resource quotas, and admission controls to enforce boundaries. Namespaces alone do not provide network isolation or a strong security boundary against hostile tenants; use separate clusters when the threat model requires them.

Name namespaces for application and environment ownership, reserve system namespaces for platform components, and verify that access, policy enforcement and quota behavior match the intended boundary. This control implements namespace protections after the separate tenant-isolation architecture decision.

items.text: Specify the security context of your pod/container
items.description:
For Linux workloads, run as non-root, disallow privilege escalation, drop all capabilities and add back only justified exceptions, use RuntimeDefault seccomp, and make the root filesystem read-only where compatible. Avoid privileged containers, host namespaces, and hostPath mounts. Apply equivalent OS-specific controls for Windows rather than assuming Linux settings apply.

Use dedicated least-privilege service accounts and set automountServiceAccountToken: false when Kubernetes API credentials are unnecessary. This does not replace the explicit projected token used by Microsoft Entra Workload ID. Provide bounded writable volumes where the application requires them and document reviewed exceptions.

items.text: Ensure your manifests respect good practices
items.description:
Render Helm or Kustomize manifests in CI, validate their schemas and supported API versions against the target AKS version, and check security, requests, probes, and deployment policies before promotion. Use server-side dry runs where safe and enforce critical requirements with admission policy rather than relying only on developer linting.

Test rendered output against a representative target cluster to catch admission, permissions and scheduling errors. A formatter improves readability but is not evidence that APIs are supported or that the deployment is safe.

items.text: Conduct Dockerfile scanning to ensure Docker Image Security Best Practices
items.description: Define and lint a container build baseline: trusted maintained base images, non-root execution, multi-stage builds, minimal runtime contents, and no embedded credentials. Use build-time secret mounts instead of copying secrets into layers; deleting them in a later layer does not remove them from image history.

items.text: Scan built container images in CI before promotion
items.description: Scan the final image digest, including OS and application dependencies, before promotion and retain the result with the release. Integrate scanning into CI; registry or runtime scanning alone is not a synchronous build gate and cannot establish that an image is vulnerability-free.

items.text: Enforce risk-based vulnerability gates for image releases
items.description:
Gate image promotion using documented vulnerability severity, exploitability, exposure, and remediation deadlines. Record time-limited exceptions with owners and compensating controls.

Do not automatically allow a critical vulnerability merely because no vendor fix exists. Require explicit risk acceptance, consider replacing or removing the vulnerable component, and rescan retained and deployed image digests as new advisories appear.

items.text: Compliance enforcement of Docker Image Builds
items.description:
Evaluate image configuration and rendered deployment manifests against a documented security baseline before release, and enforce critical runtime settings through admission policy.

Check non-root execution, privilege escalation, capabilities, host access, and approved image sources. An exposed port alone does not establish a compliance violation, and Azure Policy admission checks do not replace Dockerfile or build-time scanning.

items.text: Assess application readiness before containerization
items.description: Assess runtime and operating-system support, external dependencies, state, licensing, health endpoints, and shutdown behavior before moving an application into containers. Select currently supported migration or build tooling for the application stack; automated repackaging does not establish production readiness or remove the need for testing.

items.text: Apply the right deployment type to your application
items.description: Choose Deployment for replaceable services, StatefulSet for workloads requiring stable identity and storage, and Job or CronJob for finite or scheduled work. Configure rolling update surge/unavailable settings, readiness, rollout deadlines, and rollback procedures to match the workload and available capacity.

items.text: Don't use naked pods
items.description:
Manage production pods with a Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, or other appropriate controller. Standalone pods are not recreated on another node after node loss.

Choose the controller according to lifecycle, identity, and storage requirements; a controller recreating a pod does not by itself recover data or guarantee service availability.

items.text: Control the usage of imagePullPolicy
items.description: Set imagePullPolicy deliberately and deploy immutable digests rather than mutable latest tags. Always resolves the image reference on each start but can reuse cached layers; IfNotPresent can run a locally cached image. Test registry outages and new-node image pulls; digest pinning improves reproducibility but does not remove registry availability requirements.

items.text: Use version-controlled infrastructure as code for Azure resources
items.description: Provision AKS and its dependencies with reviewed, version-controlled Bicep, ARM, or Terraform. Secure state and deployment identities, pin supported providers and modules, detect drift, and test repeatable environment recreation. Keep credentials out of templates and repositories.

items.text: Use canary or blue/green deployments
items.description:
Applicability: Applies when application-release risk and availability targets require progressive traffic shifting or parallel application versions.

Use canary or blue/green application releases where the risk justifies additional capacity and routing complexity. Define health and business-metric gates, progressive traffic shifts, rollback, and backward-compatible database changes. These strategies reduce release risk but do not guarantee availability during cluster upgrades.

items.text: Evaluate Dapr when its building blocks fit the application
items.description:
Applicability: Applies when Dapr is installed or an assessed application requirement justifies its building blocks; Dapr adoption is not a readiness requirement.

Consider Dapr for service invocation, pub/sub, state, or other supported building blocks when it reduces application complexity. Evaluate sidecar resources, component authentication, mTLS, supported versions, operations, and failure modes; adopting Dapr is optional and does not ensure uptime during cluster upgrades.

items.text: Design retries, timeouts, and idempotency for dependency failures
items.description: Set bounded request timeouts, retry budgets with exponential backoff and jitter, and circuit breakers where appropriate. Make retried operations idempotent and support graceful degradation. Test dependency throttling and outages so retries and autoscaling do not amplify failure.

items.text: Scan the container image against vulnerabilities
items.description: Scan OS packages and application dependencies in built, stored, and deployed image digests, and rescan as vulnerability intelligence changes. Assign remediation owners and deadlines and rebuild affected images. Scanning identifies known issues; a clean result is not proof that an image is secure.

items.text: Allow deploying containers only from known registries
items.description: Enforce approved registry and repository paths with admission policy, including init and ephemeral containers. Restrict who can push or import into those repositories and combine source allowlists with digest and signature verification. Egress filtering is defense in depth, not a substitute for admission enforcement because cached images can run without a pull.

items.text: Block promotion and redeployment of images with newly discovered issues
items.description:
Continuously reassess image digests after publication and block promotion or new deployment when they violate policy. Use a supported admission and registry-access workflow rather than assuming a registry scan automatically quarantines images.

Track affected running workloads and cached images, rebuild and redeploy fixed digests, and document emergency exceptions. Blocking new image pulls does not stop existing containers or prevent cached images from being reused; coordinate containment with incident response.

items.text: Use least-privilege identity-based access to container registries
items.description: Use separate identities for image publishing and pulling; disable the ACR admin account unless explicitly required. Grant the AKS kubelet managed identity pull-only permissions, not the application workload identity. Use AcrPull for registry RBAC mode; ABAC-enabled registries require Container Registry Repository Reader and do not support az aks --attach-acr. Scope repository permissions where supported.

items.text: Enforce the required container registry network access boundary
items.description:
Applicability: Applies when the registry threat model or network policy requires private connectivity or restricted public endpoints; private endpoint adoption alone is not a readiness requirement.

Enforce the registry access boundary required by the threat model. For private access, use ACR Premium Private Link, configure private DNS and connectivity to registry and regional data endpoints, and disable public network access after validation. If private connectivity is not required, select an appropriate SKU with explicitly authorized public access rather than requiring Premium solely to pass this check.

Test image pulls from every node pool and DR region, plus CI builds and imports. Verify permitted and denied paths and that no public bypass remains where public access is prohibited. A private endpoint alone neither disables public access nor replaces identity-based authorization.

items.text: Use minimal, maintained runtime images
items.description:
Use a supported minimal or distroless runtime image appropriate for the application, architecture, and OS. Remove build tools and unused packages, run as non-root, and rebuild regularly from maintained bases.

Distroless images reduce attack surface but do not prevent exploitation or container escape. Validate certificates, runtime dependencies, patch availability, and a controlled debugging workflow rather than adding a shell to the production image.

items.text: Refresh container when base image is updated
items.description: Track base-image and dependency updates, including digest-pinned bases, and automate rebuilds followed by tests, scanning, signing, and staged redeployment. Updating a base image or rebuilding an application does not patch already-running containers; promote and deploy the new digest and retain a tested rollback image.

items.text: Sign OCI artifacts and verify trusted publishers before deployment
items.description: Sign released image digests and other OCI artifacts using supported tooling such as Notation. Verify integrity and trusted publisher identity in build and deployment workflows, and enforce verification at admission where supported. Define trust policies, certificate rotation, revocation response, and narrowly scoped exceptions; merely storing a signature in ACR does not enforce trust.

items.text: Retain SBOMs and build provenance linked to immutable image digests
items.description: Generate software bills of materials and build provenance for releases, associate them with the exact OCI image digest, and retain them with signatures and scan evidence. Record source revision, builder identity, and dependencies for incident investigation. Protect build identities and verify evidence before promotion; an SBOM alone does not establish image integrity or absence of vulnerabilities.
